notes: Cusco Quechua (Qusqu-Qullaw), the Southern Quechua variety of the Cusco region, Peru. Written in the official trivocalic alphabet (a, i, u): the five-vowel Spanish-influenced spelling with ⟨e o⟩ is explicitly NOT modelled here, since ⟨e o⟩ spell the uvular-conditioned allophones of /i u/ that this spec derives by rule instead (Wikipedia, Cusco Quechua). Cusco has the full three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates — plain, aspirated ⟨Ch⟩ and ejective ⟨C'⟩ — which the orthography writes with the digraph/apostrophe series ⟨ph th chh kh qh⟩ and ⟨p' t' ch' k' q'⟩; each spells ONE segment, so each earns its grapheme key (AGENTS.md §2 test 2). ⟨ll⟩ /ʎ/ and ⟨ñ⟩ /ɲ/ are likewise single palatal segments. The uvular vowel-lowering (/a i u/ → [ɑ ɛ ɔ] next to /q qʰ qʼ/) is expressed in the rule layer, never by enumerating vowel+uvular keys. Contrast quy (Ayacucho), which lacks both marked stop series and has /χ/ rather than /q/. ⟨b d g f⟩ are carried because running text — child-directed speech above all — is full of Spanish loans that spell them (sunbiru, banka, profesor), and without the keys the engine silently drops the letter and returns a shorter word; this holds regardless of the loan consonants' phonemic status. Sustained borrowing from Spanish may have made /b d ɡ f/ phonemic for Cusco speakers, monolinguals included (Cusihuamán 1976, cited via Wikipedia, Cusco Quechua). ⟨e o⟩ stay out: in this alphabet they are the lowered allophones the rule layer already derives, so admitting them as vowel keys would let a loan spelling override the rule that the trivocalic orthography exists to encode.
